raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old man with no medical history living in Paris, France, went to the local emergency room in November 2018 with sudden onset of psychotic symptoms (paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations and major anxiety) associated with fever, cough and general asthenia. He had no psychiatric history apart from an anxious personality and a mild tobacco and cannabis consumption and was not taking any medication. He had travelled in Greece for one week and had returned ten days before the first symptoms. He reported having unprotected sex with a man 2 months before and during his travel.
On admission, he had fever (38.5 C), pharyngitis, oral candidiasis and skin rash. Laboratory values revealed increased C-reactive protein (18 mg/L), mild anemia (10.5 g/dL) with low reticulocytes count (37 G/L), lymphopenia (500/mm3), neutropenia down to 600/mm3 and thrombocytopenia (90 G/L). HIV-1 serology returned positive, confirmed by immunoblot, with a viral load of 5.47 million copies/mL and a CD4+ T-cells count of 90/mm3. Neuroleptic drugs (cyamemazine, risperidone) and benzodiazepines were introduced to treat psychotic and anxious symptoms. He was transferred to our Infectious Diseases Department. HIV blood viral load at admission (2 weeks after first symptoms) was at 6.85 million copies/mL with a blood CD4+ T-cells count of 30/mm3 and a global lymphopenia (including CD8+ and NK cells). The immunoblot showed an uncommon band pattern (gp120 and gp41 reactivity, weak ambiguous reactivity to p24 and p31, no reactivity to other antigens), which could have been consistent with acute primary infection. He never had any HIV infection screening in the past. The research of past blood tests showed a normal lymphocytes count (1.4 G/L) a year ago. Of note, his recent partner was just diagnosed with HIV infection as well.
Lumbar puncture, electroencephalography and cerebral MRI showed no abnormality. Thoraco-abdominal and pelvic CT revealed homogenous hepatosplenomegaly and few parenchymatous interstitial pulmonary lesions (micronodules and reticulations). Sputum cultures and bronchoalveolar lavage showed no Pneumocystis nor tuberculosis infection. No co-infection with HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, toxoplasmosis nor syphilis was found. EBV and CMV viral loads were undetectable. Genotypic testing found a CRF19-cpx strain. Combined anti-retroviral therapy (cART) was introduced 2 weeks after diagnosis, consisting in tenofovir, emtricitabine and raltegravir, and Pneumocystis pneumonia was prevented by cotrimoxazole.
Despite cART and neuroleptic drugs, psychotic symptoms and fever persisted associated with chills, sweats and a neurological disorder occurred with bilateral muscle rigidity. The worsening of his clinical state required intensive care. A neuroleptic malignant syndrome was diagnosed, and extrapyramidal syndrome recovered after stopping neuroleptic treatment, but fever, chills and night sweats persisted. At this time, blood tests showed worsening pancytopenia (anemia 7.0 g/dL, platelets count 50 G/L, neutropenia 600/mm3), hyperferritinemia, elevated liver enzymes and mild elevated triglyceridemia. We hypothesized that the patient had a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by an acute primary HIV infection. Sternal bone marrow aspiration was performed showing signs of macrophages activation without hemophagocytosis. No Leishmania was found on bone marrow aspirate smears and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex PCR was negative. An empiric treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins 1 g/kg for 2 days was administered; no clinical response was observed.
Finally, a bone marrow biopsy was performed showing hemophagocytosis, confirming HLH, and moreover, revealing the presence of Leishmania spp ( Figure 1 ), with a low parasitic load. Serology was also positive for Leishmania infantum antibodies by immune-enzymatic screening technique, confirmed by Western-Blot assay. Molecular species identification confirmed a Leishmania infantum strand.
Intravenous liposomal amphotericin B was administered at 4 mg/kg/day on five consecutive days followed by five weekly administrations, allowing complete clinical recovery and pancytopenia recovery. Patient was discharged, no secondary prophylaxis against VL was prescribed. Viral load decreased to 75 copies/mL and CD4+ T-cells count increased to 213/mm3 two months after cART initiation and viral load was undetectable with CD4+ T-cells count at 345/mm3 after 6 months ( Figure 2 ), with no sign of VL relapse. After 24 months of follow-up, no VL relapse was observed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old man in Paris, France, presented in November 2018 with sudden-onset acute psychosis (paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, and severe anxiety) accompanied by fever, cough, and generalized asthenia 10 days after returning from Greece.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days after returning from a 1-week trip to Greece—and following unprotected sexual intercourse with a man 2 months prior and during his trip—the patient presented to the emergency room with acute paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, severe anxiety, fever, cough, and asthenia. He was newly diagnosed with primary/acute CRF19-cpx HIV-1 infection (viral load 5.47–6.85 million copies/mL, CD4 count dropping from 90 to 30/mm3) and treated with neuroleptics (cyamemazine, risperidone), benzodiazepines, combined antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir), and prophylactic co-trimoxazole. Despite stopping neuroleptics after an ICU admission for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (bilateral muscle rigidity), his high fevers, chills, night sweats, and worsening pancytopenia persisted.
subjective.past_medical_history: Anxious personality trait; mild tobacco and cannabis use; no prior medical or psychiatric history (normal lymphocyte count of 1.4 G/L 1 year earlier). Epidemiological history: Travel to Greece 10 days prior to symptom onset; unprotected sex with a male partner (who was also newly diagnosed with HIV).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, severe anxiety, fever (38.5 °C), chills, night sweats, cough, asthenia, pharyngitis, oral thrush, skin rash, and transient neuroleptic-induced muscle rigidity. Taking no baseline medications prior to admission.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Febrile at 38.5 °C, pharyngitis, oral candidiasis, skin rash, and acute psychotic agitation/delusions. Subsequent ICU course: Transient bilateral extrapyramidal muscle rigidity (neuroleptic malignant syndrome) that resolved after stopping neuroleptics.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: C-reactive protein (CRP) 18 mg/L, mild hyporegenerative anemia (Hb 10.5 g/dL, reticulocytes 37 G/L), lymphopenia (500/mm3), neutropenia (600/mm3), and thrombocytopenia (90 G/L); subsequent HLH progression showed severe pancytopenia (Hb 7.0 g/dL, platelets 50 G/L, neutrophils 600/mm3), hyperferritinemia, elevated liver transaminases, and mild hypertriglyceridemia. Virological and microbiological studies: HIV-1 serology positive with incomplete primary-infection immunoblot pattern (gp120/gp41 reactive, weak p24/p31), CRF19-cpx genotype, and plasma HIV-1 viral load 5.47 million copies/mL rising to 6.85 million copies/mL; negative HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, Toxoplasma, and syphilis serologies; undetectable EBV and CMV viral loads. Neurodiagnostics: Normal lumbar puncture/CSF, EEG, and brain MRI.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological status: Profound global lymphopenia (involving CD4+, CD8+, and NK cells) with CD4+ T-cell count 90/mm3 on arrival and 30/mm3 at 2 weeks. Thoracoabdominopelvic CT and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Homogeneous hepatosplenomegaly and sparse interstitial pulmonary micronodules and reticulations; sputum cultures and BAL were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Sternal bone marrow aspirate, bone marrow biopsy, and Leishmania workup: Initial aspirate showed macrophage activation without hemophagocytosis or Leishmania amastigotes and negative MTB PCR; subsequent core bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytosis and low-burden intracellular Leishmania spp. amastigotes, confirmed as Leishmania infantum by ELISA, Western blot serology, and molecular species identification.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Primary acute CRF19-cpx HIV-1 infection (viral load 6.85 million copies/mL, CD4 count 30/mm3) complicated by visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania infantum)-triggered hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; confirmed by bone marrow biopsy showing hemophagocytosis and Leishmania amastigotes, positive L. infantum Western blot, and molecular typing) and transient neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with Pneumocystis jirovecii and tuberculosis ruled out on BAL. Plan and clinical course: Neuroleptics were stopped, cART (tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir) and co-trimoxazole PJP prophylaxis were initiated, and after failing empiric IVIG (1 g/kg for 2 days), intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg/day for 5 consecutive days followed by 5 weekly doses) produced complete clinical and hematologic recovery without secondary leishmaniasis prophylaxis. At 6 and 24 months of follow-up, his HIV viral load was undetectable, his CD4+ count rose to 345/mm3, and he had no visceral leishmaniasis relapse.
